body_markdown:
Is this the worst era in which to be a car company executive? Well, if you ran an automaker in 1932, during the industry’s mass extinction event known as the Great Depression, or during the aftermath of this century’s financial crisis, you might say the times today aren’t so bad. The economy is holding its own and dealers retailed more than 16 million new light vehicles in the U.S. in 2025, not a terrible figure. But the stress in the C-suites has never been higher, and the horrific bills coming due from past missteps and sudden regulatory changes have battered the industry like a conga line of hurricanes.


Product portfolios have been trimmed and new models delayed as the industry finds itself short on cash and deeply unsure of the future. Fun niche models? Forget it, there’s no money and no appetite for introducing anything new other than profitable high-volume vehicles for the mainstream. And for those models, the lifespans of existing platforms and powertrains are being stretched as chief executives grow cautious, increasingly unwilling to place multi- billion-dollar bets on a marketplace deeply clouded by upheavals in technology and government mandates.


Consider the quadruple whammy the auto industry has experienced in the past decade.


## Whammy One – Self-Driving


Justin Sullivan/Getty Images


David Paul Morris/Bloomberg/Getty Images


Self-driving vehicles were supposed to be ubiquitous by now. Many manufacturers plied tens of billions of dollars into autonomous vehicle research and acquiring Silicon Valley startups in the hopes of getting ahead of the game. But those investments largely failed to pan out due to the slower-than-expected development of the technology. In 2024, General Motors alone wrote off $10 billion in losses after abandoning its Cruise autonomous vehicle division. A slow rollout of limited autonomy has whetted the appetite of drivers for more, but the rosy forecasts upon which so much was expended have proved to be costly optimism.


## Whammy Two – EVs


Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg/Getty Images


In 2017, as battery advances helped increase the range and reduce the cost of electric vehicles and tax incentives goosed their sales, most forecasts predicted EVs would be 15 to 20% of the new-vehicle market in the U.S. by 2026. California, the largest single new-car market in the United States, adopted an EV mandate requiring the complete phaseout of new internal combustion vehicles in the state by 2035. Seduced by the headlines and the temptation to follow Tesla into Wall Street’s lucrative embrace, the industry opened its collective wallet and poured hundreds of billions into electric vehicle development. Some brands committed to going all-electric by the end of the decade (2030). Today, however, both the mandate and the tax credits are gone and EV sales are stuck at about 6% of the U.S. new-vehicle market, even as they rise rapidly elsewhere in the world.


## Whammy Three – Tariffs


Getty Images


Decades of building highly streamlined international supply chains followed the signing of the North American Free Trade Agreement in 1992, the linchpin in a global trade system among industrialized nations that was largely free of tariffs. All that was thrown into chaos in 2025 with the sudden adoption of massive tariff barriers by the Trump administration. Since then, the industry has been clobbered by an estimated $35 billion in tariff costs, much of it eaten by the automakers themselves in an effort to keep prices competitive in an environment where affordability is already a heated topic. The automakers are between the proverbial rock and hard place; they can gamble billions on multi-decade commitments to bring manufacturing back to U.S. shores, or gamble billions that the tariffs will go away when the administration changes or the courts or Congress eliminate them.


## Whammy Four – China


Ju Huanzong/Xinhua/Getty Images


The current world leader in EV development and sales is suffering a years-long slowdown in its home market, ratcheting up pressure among its 129 domestic car brands to flood the world with cheap exports. It’s kill or be killed in China—one major forecasting company, AlixPartners, predicts that only 15 of those brands will still be viable by 2030 after failures and mergers. In the meantime, the deluge of low-cost Chinese electric cars into markets that allow them, particularly Europe, has created an existential crisis in the legacy auto industry. Volkswagen stunned its German employees and shareholders in July by announcing that it was cutting up to half of its models, closing four plants in Europe, and laying off 100,000 workers by the end of the decade, partly due to Chinese competition.


In February, Chrysler owner Stellantis announced a staggering $26 billion write-down to cover losses generated by its reversing course on its electrification strategy, while Ford said its earnings took a $19.5 billion hit due to slowing sales of electric vehicles. The company cut its model lineup and reorganized (again) to face new realities. All that money must come from somewhere, and at least some of it is being cut from new-product programs.


In much of the world, traditional automakers are struggling to contend with polished new Chinese EVs like the BYD Seal.


Nick French


Long renowned for establishing the five-year product renewal cadence that kept their vehicles fresh and perennially on top of the sales charts, Japanese automakers are beating a retreat. After suddenly canceling three electric models earlier this year that were reportedly fully engineered, tooled up at a factory in Ohio, and nearly ready for the showroom, Honda reported an annual loss of $2.7 billion, its first loss since the 77-year-old company listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in 1957. It subsequently emerged that Honda has delayed new versions of the Accord, Odyssey, HR-V and various sister Acura models until 2030.


Likewise, a Japanese newspaper broke a story late in 2025 that Toyota is also looking to extend its platform lifespans, from the five years that became the standard in the 1980s to nine years. The automaker acknowledged that longer lifespans would give companies more time to sort out electrical architectures and software issues—software has become the most important and most complex component in any modern vehicle—and would make cars more affordable. Additionally, it would give automakers time to see which way the market is going before making their next move.


Toyota


In a moment of high fuel prices, hybrids are red hot in the U.S., seeming to offer buyers the best of both the electrified and internally combusted worlds. Toyota, which placed its bet on hybrids a while back, is well situated with hybrid versions of many of its bestselling vehicles. Meanwhile, two of the world’s largest automakers, General Motors and Volkswagen, the latter of which hasn’t sold a hybrid in the U.S. since 2016, went all-in on full electrification. They have been caught flat-footed.


But will hybrids stay hot enough long enough to merit spending more billions to rush them to market? Executives trying to read the tea leaves find it impossible to predict. Ford CEO Jim Farley told reporters late last year that the company is pursuing a two-pronged strategy of hybrids and electrics so that if one triumphs over the other in the coming years, “we have lots of flexibility.” Meanwhile, GM CEO Mary Barra has said publicly that the company is sticking to its EV plan, partly to stay ahead of intense competition from China, and partly out of the expectation that EVs will ultimately win out. No doubt, it’s also partly because the cost of changing course yet again is too high, especially if you believe that hybrids are a passing phase, just a transition technology to full EVs. The U.S. market is currently walled off from Chinese imports by a high tariff barrier, but tariffs are being litigated in the federal courts and national elections in 2026 and 2028 may upend the whole situation.


> Companies have learned to take a wait-and-see approach.


Volvo expected federal incentives to bring the price of its Chinese-built EX30 below $30K. Instead, the end of those incentives–and the addition of tariffs–forced the EV’s discontinuation in the United States.


Nick French


How would you write a five-year business plan for a major automaker knowing that in two years the country could possibly swap its tariff-loving Republican president for a Democratic Socialist? Or a Republican who despises tariffs? Or a Democrat who thinks some tariffs are OK but solar and wind should power a fully electrified economy? In an era when great changes happen suddenly and federal regulatory policy reverses on a whim, car companies have learned through bitter experience to take a wait-and-see approach.


“We’re in an era of volatility of regulations that I’ve never seen in 30 years at General Motors,” said Mike Kociba, assistant chief engineer for the new Gen-6 GM small-block V-8 at the unveiling of the 2027 Corvette Grand Sport. When the small-block redesign program was initiated around 2020, Kociba said he was told it would be the last V-8 that GM would ever make. Since then, the company has pulled back on its electrification drive and now, he says, “I’m busier than ever.”


Vast fortunes were lost trying to get ahead of change, so the industry seems cowed at present into waiting to see where time, politics, and the market will take it. Said Kociba, “My ability to predict the weather is better than my ability to predict which way things will go in the next few years.”
